source.title: The role of regularization in classification of high-dimensional noisy Gaussian mixture
source.authors: Francesca Mignacco; Florent Krzakala; Yue M. Lu; Pierfrancesco Urbani; Lenka Zdeborov'a

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes test/generalization error around interpolation in high-dimensional linear classifiers, using a Gaussian-mixture model and regularized empirical-risk minimization rather than deep networks.
record.gate_note: The paper's own results sweep the sample-to-dimension ratio α and regularization and report generalization-error curves. It also discusses cited double-descent work, which is not recorded as a result. Numerical curve values in Figures 1–4 are not tabulated, so those entries are recorded as figure only.
record.test_reason: The paper derives exact asymptotic test-error curves for ridge-regularized square, hinge and logistic linear classifiers on a noisy two-Gaussian mixture. It sweeps α=n/d and λ. Its own results show a sample-wise interpolation peak at low λ that regularization removes. That bears on V3 and on V6's regularization part, in a new setting: linear classification rather than deep networks.
record.authors_conclusion: The authors conclude three things. Regularization strongly shapes performance: for balanced clusters, λ→∞ reaches Bayes-optimal error, while for unbalanced clusters the optimal λ is finite and falls short of Bayes-optimal. Low regularization shows an interpolation peak or cusp (at α=1 for square loss, at the separability threshold α* for hinge/logistic) that regularization smoothly removes. Hinge and logistic losses converge to max-margin as λ→0 on separable data. The record's paraphrase is correct for the peak but omits the Bayes-optimality results, which are the main focus.
record.recipe_differences: Rigorous high-dimensional analysis and numerical simulations for regularized convex linear classifiers on noisy Gaussian mixtures; not a reproduction of the deep-network experiments in the cited original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported peak changes with regularization; the paper also studies dependence on cluster balance, but Fig. 2 fixes Δ=1 and ρ=0.5.

fits_no_version.finding: The location of the interpolation peak depends on the loss and on the data structure. For square loss it sits at n=d (α=1). For hinge/logistic it sits at the linear-separability threshold α*(Δ,ρ), which moves with cluster variance and imbalance (Fig. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The interpolation peak sits at the training-loss-vanishing (separability) threshold, whose position depends on loss and data distribution rather than on parameter count alone.

record.problems: The relevant generalization-error curves are shown in figures rather than tabulated, so exact values and uncertainty estimates are unavailable. The peak/regularization sweep is in a specific high-dimensional Gaussian-mixture linear-classification model; simulations are finite-dimensional checks of asymptotic formulas.

untested.parts: The paper frames its sweep as samples per dimension (α), not capacity past interpolation. No capacity-wise curve is reported, though at fixed n, α is inverse to d.
No single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Label-noise or variance (Δ) dependence of the peak height, and multiple or triple peaks, are not tested. Fig. 2 fixes Δ=1 and ρ=0.5.

missing.what: Low-λ (1e-7) square and logistic curves versus α with peaks at α=1 and α*, alongside optimal-λ curves that match Bayes-optimal and show no peak, plus simulations at d=1000.
Unbalanced clusters (ρ=0.2). Low-λ versus optimal-λ square-loss curves, with optimal λ finite and error bounded above Bayes-optimal. Whether the peak vanishes under optimal λ here is not stated.

record.verdict_notes: This is an analytic, asymptotic study with finite-d simulation checks; all curve values are figure-only. It is not an original source. The peak here is sample-wise (α=n/d), so it bears on V3 rather than V1 or V4. Δ>0 gives intrinsic label noise, but noise is not varied in the peak analysis. Tranche changed from T2 to T3: a new setting, linear Gaussian-mixture classification.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over training epochs or training time.
The sample-size effect is studied through α=n/d in a high-dimensional Gaussian-mixture classification setting; it is not tested in deep networks or across other data-generating settings.
The paper does not sweep model capacity past interpolation; it sweeps the sample-to-dimension ratio for linear classifiers.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and sample axes.

The paper tests how regularization affects the interpolation peak for fixed-noise settings. It does not test whether varying label noise causes the peak, whether peaks split into multiple peaks, or the broader claim about optimally tuned regularization across settings.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective number of parameters.

relationships.condition: Low regularization (λ=1e-8), square and logistic loss, Δ=1, ρ=0.5
relationships.reason: Error peaks at α=1 for square loss and is non-monotonic in α at α* for logistic. So more samples raise error near the threshold (r1, r17).
relationships.display_finding: Error peaked at α = 1 with square loss and varied nonmonotonically around α* with logistic loss, including increases with more samples.

source_check.reason: The text explicitly describes square-loss peaking at α=1 and logistic nonmonotonicity; Figure 2 identifies the low-regularization setting in r1 and r17.

relationships.reason: Described only as a 'peak/cusp' or 'kink' at α*. A rise in error with more data is not clearly stated (r9).
relationships.display_finding: A cusp or kink occurs at α*, without establishing an interval where additional data increases error.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: The unresolved hinge cusp in r9 establishes neither a harmful increasing interval nor its absence or attenuation. Insufficient evidence for V3 is not evidence limiting its scope.

relationships.reason: Regularization smooths the peak and at λ=10 removes it, so more data stops hurting. The effect depends on the choice of λ (r2–r8, r10–r16, r18–r24).
relationships.display_finding: Regularization smooths the peak and removes it at λ=10, eliminating the harmful sample-size region.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: The sweep explicitly establishes regularization-dependent smoothing and disappearance, qualifying V3. The reason must omit disappearance specifically at λ=10 and must not assign partial or absent states to every individual intermediate λ.

relationships.condition: Δ=1, ρ=0.5, square/hinge/logistic losses, sweeping λ
relationships.reason: The peak present at λ=1e-8 shrinks with λ and is gone at λ=10. Optimally tuned λ reaches Bayes-optimal error without a peak (r1–r24; text on Fig. 1–2).
relationships.display_finding: The peak at λ = 10^-8 shrank and disappeared by λ = 10, while optimal λ attained Bayes-optimal error without a peak.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Δ=1, ρ=0.5, square/hinge/logistic losses, sweeping λ
source_check.reason: Figure 2 and its discussion explicitly establish disappearance with regularization; the balanced asymptotic optimum approaches Bayes error as λ→∞. This supports V6's regularization component, without establishing a λ=10 cutoff, a noise mechanism or multiple peaks.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.reason: The sweep explicitly establishes regularization-dependent smoothing and disappearance, qualifying V3. The reason must omit disappearance specifically at λ=10 and must not assign partial or absent states to every individual intermediate λ.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Δ=1, ρ=0.5, square/hinge/logistic losses, sweeping λ
labels.reason: Figure 2 and its discussion explicitly establish disappearance with regularization; the balanced asymptotic optimum approaches Bayes error as λ→∞. This supports V6's regularization component, without establishing a λ=10 cutoff, a noise mechanism or multiple peaks.

relation.reason: Its own generalization-error curves as functions of α=n/d and λ directly bear on V3 and the regularization component of V6.

tranche.reason: The study supplies its own asymptotic results in a noisy Gaussian-mixture setting with convex linear classifiers, demonstrating sample-wise interpolation features and their regularization dependence.

source_check.notes: The individual curve shapes are unavailable in the extracted text; their listed λ values do not establish per-λ states. Bayes optimality at λ→∞ requires exactly balanced clusters in the proportional asymptotic limit; finite-size systems require tuning.

statements.correction: Gaussian-mixture classification; Δ=1; ρ=0.5; square, hinge and logistic losses; Figure 2 lists λ=10; regularization smoothly removes the peak/cusp; numerical disappearance cutoff unstated; intermediate smoothing alone does not establish monotonicity.
statements.problem: The Gaussian-mixture result establishes smoothing and eventual disappearance, but does not explicitly identify λ=10 as the disappearance point.
